attrs.evidence: probe_reread_v13_repro.mjs, paired and gating: 2/2 reproduce against frozen v0.12.0 copies of execute() and accept() — the authority issues psem-82eee05e… (const 5), executes psem-3b198d80… (const 999), the native worker returns 999, and acceptance of that result under a fresh time-varying request returns {ok:true, validated:true, implementation_provenance:'observed'} while the frozen issued request refuses it as result-program-mismatch. 5/5 confined live: a time-varying request is read EXACTLY ONCE by execute() and the program that runs is the one authorized; acceptance reads a time-varying request once and a time-varying result once; wasIssued() returns the deep-frozen issued request and a stranger authority still gets grant-not-issued-by-this-authority and no request; a function-carrying result, a ProgramRegistry in the request slot and a closure-carrying intent each die at the entry rather than halfway through; and the ladder is one frozen record of seven rungs. derive_realm_battery.mjs case 'every-entrypoint-reads-its-argument-once' enumerates nine entrypoints and measures reads against a one-read-per-field floor: 7/7, 1/1, 11/11, 11/11, 11/11, 18/18, 11/11, 18/18, 2/2. Reintroducing the defect in execute() alone moves that to 33/11 and the case names the offending entrypoint. P-7c: 3/3 frozen breaches and 6/6 live confinements in the same probe — the frozen v0.2.1 read ordering splits the keyed request from the executed one, and the live host reads its invocation exactly once, answers 5 for the request it keyed, and holds the observation under the bytes that ran and not under the ones that did not. derive_realm_battery.mjs case 'meta-operations-stop-at-one-traversal' hands twelve entrypoints — including the reusable exports — a RECURSIVELY Proxy-wrapped argument counting ownKeys, getOwnPropertyDescriptor, getPrototypeOf, has and get, and requires each to equal a single ownCanonical traversal exactly (e.g. wasIssued/req gOPD:11 get:11 getPrototypeOf:6 ownKeys:6).
attrs.statement: EVERY AUTHORITY OPERATION CONSUMES EITHER AN AUTHORITY-OWNED OBJECT OR ONE CANONICAL SNAPSHOT MADE AT ENTRY. NO TRUST DECISION AUTHENTICATES ONE READ OF EXTERNAL STATE AND EXERCISES AUTHORITY USING ANOTHER. derivation.owned-snapshot@1 stated this rule for structures BECOMING authority state and was correct; this is the same rule reaching method ARGUMENTS, where it had never been applied. wasIssued(req) hashed one read of every field and proved 'these bytes are the request I issued'; execute() then read the caller's object again for the implementation family, again when the host canonicalised the invocation, and again when the worker structured-cloned it. A request whose program_sem_id answers const(5) to the first read and const(999) to every read after it is therefore ISSUED as one program and EXECUTED as another. Both programs are genuinely in the authority's own registry, so nothing is malformed, no identity is forged and nothing fails closed: acceptance re-derives 999 against 999, finds the provenance of an execution the authority really drove, and returns implementation_provenance 'observed' for a result the authority never authorized. THE SAME RESULT PAIRED WITH THE FROZEN ISSUED REQUEST IS REFUSED as result-program-mismatch, which is what makes this a forgery rather than fail-closed hygiene — the entire difference is the caller's retained ownership. THE REPAIR IS NOT A FRESHER HASH. Hashing again would authenticate a second read and leave a third. The issuance table keeps the REQUEST and not merely its identity, because a table of hashes can answer 'were these bytes issued?' and cannot answer 'what did I issue?', and every method that needed the second question had no choice but to re-read the caller; wasIssued() returns that owned request and execute() and accept() read it. THE RESULT SIDE WAS CLOSED IN THE SAME ROUND, ONE ARGUMENT TO THE RIGHT, without waiting for its own witness: `res` was consulted by six checks in sequence, and a caller who cannot vary the request while it is validated can still vary the result. Seven rungs, one shape — LABEL, NAME, ACTION, SEMANTIC ORACLE, AUTHORITY-BEARING OBJECT, MUTABLE DATA READ TWICE, MUTABLE DATA AUTHENTICATED ONCE — and @6 and @7 are one rule at two moments: validate X then store X', authenticate X then act with X'. The mechanism is one exported ownCanonical() called at the top of every method taking a non-root data argument, and the enforcement is a battery case that enumerates the authority's entrypoints and fails when any argument is read more than once per field, because a law applied only where a witness has been written is a law with the reach of its witnesses. AND THE OBLIGATION BELONGS TO THE ENTRYPOINT, NOT TO ITS POLITEST CALLER. ObservedExecutionHost.run() keyed the observation over canonicalBytes(invocation) and then handed the same live object to the transport, so an invocation honest on read 1 and hostile on read 2 was KEYED under one request and EXECUTED as another, leaving a true-looking observation for an execution that did not happen — in the table round 23 built precisely so that relabelling would move the key. That path is unreachable through DerivationAuthority.execute, whose invocation is assembled from owned parts; the host is nonetheless exported, FilmAuthority and lowering_check drive it directly, and it writes the observation table, so it is an authority operation carrying the rule itself (P-7c). THE REUSABLE VALIDATORS CARRY THE SAME OBLIGATION AT THEIR OWN EDGE. checkRequest, checkIntent, checkResult, deriveLocally and validateForeignResult reread their arguments field by field — one checkRequest call over a Proxy-wrapped request touched ownKeys 2, getOwnPropertyDescriptor 10, getPrototypeOf 1, get 13 and has 1 — so 'a pure function over data the caller already owns' is the second half of a sentence whose first half was a precondition nothing enforced. The implementations are named ...Owned and the precondition is mechanical inside the authority, which passes only issued/ownRes/ownIntent; the exported names snapshot once and delegate, so a second authority built on them cannot recreate P-7 without writing new trust logic. This is an API-boundary hazard predicted by the law, not a false verdict, and it is deliberately not numbered as a rung. AND HISTORICAL FACT IS NOT A FUNCTION OF CURRENT CONFIGURATION. Acceptance rebuilt the invocation it asked the observation table about out of this.#registry.image(), so bindProgram() — an explicit, legitimate authority operation — grew that image and made the provenance of an earlier genuine execution vanish: execute(A), accept -> observed, bindProgram(B), accept the same request and result -> implementation-provenance-unavailable. It fails closed and forges nothing, and it is still wrong, because unrelated future installation must not erase the evidence of what previously ran. execute() now records the canonical invocation bytes THE HOST KEYED, acceptance looks those up, and the records are a list because the same request run before and after a bind is two genuinely different invocations and both happened; observations across them are MERGED rather than first-hit, for the round-24 reason that reporting one launch as though it were the only one overclaims. DECLARED OPEN: object-form canonicalisation MAY INVOKE JavaScript accessor and Proxy behaviour while capturing its snapshot — reading {get x(){}} executes a function, and a Proxy runs ownKeys/getOwnPropertyDescriptor/getPrototypeOf/has/get traps during serialisation. What is established is that no such behaviour SURVIVES the snapshot or participates in any later authority decision, measured as a full-trap surface equal to exactly one ownCanonical traversal. The stronger property — no hostile same-realm code executes at ingestion at all — is unreachable for any API whose boundary is an arbitrary JavaScript object, and needs a serialized-wire boundary (canonical text -> authority-owned parser -> data), which is not built. Relatedly, the read-count enumeration is a REGRESSION DETECTOR AND NOT A TERMINATING PROOF: Object.keys(x) twice leaves an accessor's read count at zero while touching the object twice, so a field-read counter sees only the `get` category and the meta-operation instrument covers the rest.
